clue.text: In modern warfare it would suggest that he carried a tank

definitions.text: In modern warfare it would suggest that he carried a tank

parts.words: In modern warfare it would suggest that he carried a tank
parts.note: a squire who carried a knight's armour; in tank warfare 'armour' means tanks, so the title sounds like a man lugging a tank

explanation.surface: A joke about an old military title read with modern eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: Today 'armour' is the army's word for its tanks and armoured vehicles, so the old title reads as if its holder hauled one about.
explanation.definitionFit: The historical title for an attendant who carried a knight's protective gear, read literally with the modern military sense.

clue.text: If a tar capsizes there's a following

definitions.text: If a tar capsizes there's a following

indicators.note: the lone letter is placed after the turned-over words
a boat that capsizes turns over, so the words are read upside down, which in a down entry means bottom to top

parts.note: a tar is an old word for a sailor; the scan's 'car' is a misread

explanation.surface: If a sailor goes overboard, something comes after.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan reads 'car', but 'tar' (a sailor) is needed: IF A TAR turned over gives RATAFI, and 'there's a following' adds A after it. The 1945 clue has no separate definition of the almond liqueur.
explanation.definitionFit: The letters built name an almond-flavoured cordial, also a small almond biscuit; the clue offers nothing else to define it.

clue.text: They make Sonia bolt

definitions.text: They
definitions.note: the answer is plural, things offered up as sacrifice

indicators.note: the letters of the two names are made into something new, rearranged into the answer

explanation.surface: Some unnamed things frighten a girl called Sonia into running away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bolt' looks like a verb (Sonia runs off), but it is just fodder: SONIA BOLT rearranged gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Offerings presented to God are what the pronoun stands for; the clue leans on the wordplay to pin it down.

clue.text: Evidently not built for track events

definitions.text: Evidently not built for track events

parts.words: Evidently not built for track events
parts.note: a car or bicycle made for ordinary highway use, its very name showing it is not a racing-track machine

explanation.surface: A remark about a vehicle unsuited to athletics or racing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'track events' suggests running, but the clue means a racing circuit; the name itself says the machine belongs on the highway.
explanation.definitionFit: An open car or bicycle for highway travel, so its name declares it was meant for streets rather than circuits.

clue.text: This hall wasn't in this college

definitions.text: This hall wasn't in this college

parts.words: This hall wasn't in this college
parts.note: one name serves both a famous London meeting hall on the Strand and an Oxford college, which are entirely separate places

explanation.surface: A tour guide pointing out that a certain hall is not part of a certain college.
explanation.walkthrough: Exeter Hall was a London venue for religious meetings; Exeter College is in Oxford. The clue plays on one name for both.
explanation.definitionFit: The cathedral city's name was borne by both a Strand assembly hall and an Oxford college, unconnected institutions.

clue.text: Send

definitions.text: Send

parts.note: to transmit payment or refer a matter onward, as when a court passes a case back

explanation.surface: A single instruction to dispatch something.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue is one plain word with no wordplay, so it is solved as a straight definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dispatching money by post or passing a case to another body are both covered by this verb.

clue.text: Suitable address for a sour boat-race critic

definitions.text: Suitable address for a sour boat-race critic

parts.words: Suitable address for a sour boat-race critic
parts.note: a famous riding track in Hyde Park whose name, taken literally, is a scathing verdict on an oarsman's effort

explanation.surface: Where a grumpy commentator on university rowing might live.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotten Row is the bridleway along the south side of Hyde Park in London; read literally it says the rowing was poor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hyde Park bridleway's name doubles as a sneering verdict on a crew's performance, making it a fitting home address.

clue.text: Concerning a round in the ring

definitions.text: Concerning

parts.note: a bout is a boxing contest in the ring

explanation.surface: Something to do with one round of a boxing match.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words introduce a topic: a book on or regarding a subject.

clue.text: A head-rest if slightly altered to start with

definitions.text: to start with
definitions.note: a dish served as the first course of a meal

indicators.note: only a small change is made to the word for a pillow, two of its letters trading places

parts.note: a bolster is a long pillow on which the head rests

explanation.surface: A pillow that, tweaked a little, becomes something else.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the B and L of BOLSTER. 'to start with' looks like a positional signal, but it is the definition: a seafood starter.
explanation.definitionFit: The shellfish is a classic first course, the dish a diner might have before the main meal.

clue.text: Is this what troops were " cut off" with ?

definitions.text: Is this what troops were " cut off" with ?

parts.words: Is this what troops were " cut off" with ?
parts.note: an army surrounded is said to be cut off; the clue pictures a medieval weapon doing the cutting literally

explanation.surface: A wry question about the phrase used when troops are isolated by the enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'cut off' in war means being surrounded, but the clue takes it literally and asks for the chopping weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A broad-headed war hatchet is the obvious tool for literally severing anything on a battlefield.

clue.text: "" Always merry and bright," for example

definitions.text: "" Always merry and bright," for example

parts.words: "" Always merry and bright," for example
parts.note: a cheerful slogan of the sort printed on a crest or adopted as a rule for living

explanation.surface: Quoting an upbeat saying as a sample.
explanation.definitionFit: A short guiding maxim adopted by a person or family; the quoted cheerful saying is one example.

clue.text: No tailor should be thus indisposed

definitions.text: No tailor should be thus
definitions.meaning: a tailor's work should fit well, so one ought never to be poor at fitting

definitions.text: indisposed
definitions.meaning: slightly ill, not in good health

explanation.surface: A tailor who should never be unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads the word as 'not fitting', as a badly cut suit; the second is the ordinary sense of out of condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being poorly or out of condition is the everyday sense; the tailoring sense is clothes that do not sit properly.

clue.text: "Notes with many a winding bout Of linked long drawn out " (Milton)

definitions.text: "Notes with many a winding bout Of linked long drawn out " (Milton)

parts.words: "Notes with many a winding bout Of linked long drawn out " (Milton)
parts.note: a line from Milton's poem L'Allegro with one word missing; the gap is filled by the word for pleasant musical quality

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank from Milton's description of music.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's L'Allegro reads 'Of linked sweetness long drawn out'; the solver supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing quotation word names the pleasant, melodious quality of the drawn-out musical notes.

clue.text: Here one can just get rid of a hang-over

definitions.text: Here

indicators.note: one letter is thrown away from the hyphenated word, just as a sufferer sheds a headache

explanation.surface: Advertising a place where you can cure a morning-after headache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get rid of' removes the G from HANGOVER. 'Here' points to a place: the German city and former kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: The pointing word stands for a location, here the German city that gave Britain its royal house.

clue.text: A cask for the card-player, musician, fencer, heraldic enthusiast or priest

definitions.text: A cask for the card-player, musician, fencer, heraldic enthusiast or priest

parts.words: A cask for the card-player, musician, fencer, heraldic enthusiast or priest
parts.note: one word means a wine cask, a run of three cards, a musical third, a fencing parry, a shield divided in three, and a canonical hour

explanation.surface: A list of hobbyists all drawn to the same barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The word has a separate meaning for each person listed: piquet sequence, organ stop or interval, the third parry, a heraldic division, the service at the third hour.
explanation.definitionFit: A word with many specialist senses, from an old wine measure to church office, covering every trade named.

clue.text: Tanning I'd expect to make me this

definitions.text: Tanning I'd expect to make me this

indicators.note: the letters are made into a new word, so the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone expecting a beating to leave them angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tanning' looks like sunbathing, but here means a thrashing; its letters with I'D rearrange to give the answer, which also describes the victim.
explanation.definitionFit: Angered at unfair treatment, exactly how a person would feel after a thrashing.

clue.text: A somewhat discredited philosopher

definitions.text: A somewhat discredited philosopher

parts.note: a Greek teacher of rhetoric whose clever but misleading reasoning earned a poor name

explanation.surface: A thinker whose reputation has slipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Greek paid teachers of argument came to stand for plausible but fallacious reasoning, hence the poor repute.

clue.text: He declined his majority, as it were

definitions.text: He declined his majority, as it were

parts.words: He declined his majority, as it were
parts.note: majority here means legal adulthood; the boy in J. M. Barrie's play refused to grow up

explanation.surface: A politician turning down an electoral majority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'majority' suggests votes, but it means coming of age; Barrie's hero is the boy who would never grow up.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrie's character famously refused ever to become an adult, so he spurned coming of age.

clue.text: So airs may be varied

definitions.text: So airs may be varied

indicators.note: the letters of the two words can be changed about into a new order

explanation.surface: A musician noting that tunes can be given variations.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1945 clue is all wordplay: SO AIRS rearranged gives the Indian province (now Odisha) with no separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The rearranged letters name a coastal state of eastern India, now spelt Odisha, the clue's only pointer to it.

clue.text: Whatever else they may be, they are not outsiders

definitions.text: Whatever else they may be, they are not outsiders

parts.words: Whatever else they may be, they are not outsiders
parts.note: prisoners or asylum residents are by definition kept indoors, so they can never be on the outside

explanation.surface: A remark about people who belong to the in-crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outsiders' suggests social misfits, but literally the residents of a prison are not outside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents of a jail or institution live within its walls, so they are literally insiders.

clue.text: Trouble in the mews

definitions.text: Trouble in the mews

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the other, the fuss sitting within the stable lane

parts.note: a mews is a row of stables, taken as written
ado means fuss or bother

explanation.surface: A disturbance in a row of converted stables.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1945 clue is wordplay only, with no separate definition. A mews is a British back street of former stables, now often smart housing.
explanation.definitionFit: Grasslands for grazing or hay are named by the letters built, with no separate defining words in the clue.

clue.text: A choice provision

definitions.text: A choice provision

parts.note: a contractual clause granting the right to choose, or simply a choice offered

explanation.surface: Something fine laid on, like select food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'choice provision' reads like quality supplies, but means an arrangement giving the right to choose.
explanation.definitionFit: An alternative available to pick, or a contract right to buy later, is literally a provision for choosing.

clue.text: money is Aladdin's lamp " (Byron)

definitions.text: money is Aladdin's lamp " (Byron)

parts.note: The missing first word is the gap to fill

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank from Byron about cash as a magic lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation from Don Juan is printed without its opening word, which the solver supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's line opens with the word that, before money, means cash in hand.

clue.text: Hardly the dish "to set before a king "

definitions.text: Hardly the dish "to set before a king "

parts.words: Hardly the dish "to set before a king "
parts.note: the nursery rhyme's blackbird pie was a dainty dish for a king; a pie of offal, eaten in submission, is the opposite

explanation.surface: A meal unfit for royalty, quoting the nursery rhyme Sing a Song of Sixpence.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase is from the rhyme's 'dainty dish to set before the king'; the answer is the lowly pie of deer offal, eaten when admitting fault.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally a pie of offal for servants, now the figurative meal of apology, so the reverse of a regal dish.

clue.text: It's found in those who become suddenly rich

definitions.text: It's found in those who become suddenly rich

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of two words, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: A trait seen among the newly wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit in suddenLY RICh; the clue gives no further definition of the poem or song words.
explanation.definitionFit: A short song-like poem, or the words of a song, is spelt by the run of letters the clue points to.

clue.text: Distracted in Hamlet

definitions.text: Distracted in Hamlet

parts.note: Hamlet speaks of memory holding a seat 'in this distracted ...', meaning his troubled head

explanation.surface: A description of the Danish prince's troubled state of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 1 Hamlet says 'while memory holds a seat in this distracted globe'; the word fills the phrase, also naming Shakespeare's theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's prince calls his head a distracted sphere, using the word that also names the playhouse.

clue.text: Burn it for battle

definitions.text: Burn it for battle

parts.note: the river-loving animal followed by a Scots word for stream names a Northumbrian battle of 1388

explanation.surface: An order to set fire to something to start a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burn' is a Scottish stream, not fire: put it after the answer and you get Otterburn, where Scots beat the English in 1388.
explanation.definitionFit: Adding the Scots stream word to the fish-eating mammal gives the name of a famous border battle.

clue.text: Beastly man or manly beast

definitions.text: Beastly man or manly beast

parts.note: a woodland creature of Greek myth, half man and half goat, and also a lecherous man

explanation.surface: A neat reversal describing a coarse fellow or a humanlike animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The goat-legged companion of Dionysus is part human, part animal, and the word also means a lustful man.

clue.text: Comment of the seed when the gardener had dealt with it

definitions.text: Comment of the seed when the gardener had dealt with it

parts.words: Comment of the seed when the gardener had dealt with it
parts.note: a sown seed would say '...', which run together is a word meaning firmly fixed in

explanation.surface: A talking seed remarking on its sowing.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as I'M PLANTED it is the seed speaking; as one word it means set firmly in place.
explanation.definitionFit: The seed's remark, run together, makes the word for something embedded or fixed in the soil.

clue.text: Characteristic of one who travels neither first nor third class ?

definitions.text: Characteristic of one who travels neither first nor third class ?

parts.words: Characteristic of one who travels neither first nor third class ?
parts.note: a habit so deep it is instinctive; the clue reads it as the temperament of a second-class rail passenger

explanation.surface: Musing on the personality of a middle-class rail traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: British trains once had first, second and third class carriages; the answer, taken literally, suits the second-class traveller.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrained habit or trait is called this idiom, here read literally as a second-class passenger's character.
